html:
(8) Meta-cognitive self-model: beliefs about one’s own channel capacity. The psychological constructs reviewed earlier–self-efficacy, locus of control, perceived autonomy–are not raw empowerment values but beliefs about empowerment: generalized, context-abstracted estimates of the agent’s capacity to influence outcomes. This implies a hierarchical representational structure in which the agent maintains not only state-by-state empowerment estimates ℰ̂(s)\hat{\mathcal{E}}(s) but also higher-order summary statistics: a trait-level prior P(ℰ)P(\mathcal{E}) reflecting the agent’s generalized expectation of controllability across contexts, and domain-specific priors P(ℰ∣domain)P(\mathcal{E} \mid \text{domain}) (e.g., "I am generally effective in social interactions but not in athletic contexts"). These meta-estimates function as priors on empowerment that modulate the agent’s willingness to engage with a new context before any direct empowerment estimation has occurred: an agent with a strong prior of high self-efficacy will enter novel situations and begin "probing the channel," while an agent with a helplessness-shaped prior (P(ℰ)≈δ(0)P(\mathcal{E}) \approx \delta(0)) will avoid engagement entirely, foreclosing the possibility of disconfirming evidence and creating the self-perpetuating motivational collapse observed in depression 1. This meta-cognitive layer also introduces a learning rate problem: the prior must be responsive enough to update from new evidence of controllability (allowing recovery from helplessness via mastery experiences 2) but stable enough to resist transient fluctuations in experienced I(A;S′)I(A;S')–and pathological states may correspond to miscalibrated learning rates (too fast →\rightarrow fragile confidence; too slow →\rightarrow entrenched helplessness).

Neural architecture; how is it evolutionarily instantiated as an architectural prior?

Maintaining hierarchical beliefs about one’s own channel capacity–a trait-level prior P(ℰ)P(\mathcal{E}) and domain-specific priors P(ℰ∣domain)P(\mathcal{E} \mid \text{domain})–requires three architectural ingredients: (a) a self-referential representational substrate that encodes stable, context-abstracted properties of the agent itself (not just the current state of the world), (b) a hierarchical abstraction mechanism that distills episode-level empowerment experiences into progressively more general summary statistics, and (c) precision-weighted updating that controls how rapidly these meta-estimates revise in light of new controllability evidence.

The neural substrate most consistently implicated in trait-level self-referential representation is medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), particularly ventromedial and dorsomedial subdivisions. A large convergent literature–spanning fMRI self-referential judgment paradigms, lesion studies, and meta-analyses–supports that mPFC is preferentially recruited when subjects evaluate enduring self-attributes (personality traits, generalized competence beliefs, autobiographical identity) as opposed to other-referential or semantic judgments, and that damage to mPFC impairs the coherent organization of self-knowledge 3, 4, 5. This positions mPFC as the natural locus for a generalized empowerment prior P(ℰ)P(\mathcal{E}): it is the same region that (i) monitors real-time controllability (vmPFC→\rightarrowDRN gating, per bullet 7), and (ii) encodes generalized state value (vmPFC value signals in model-based decision-making), making it architecturally efficient for trait-level controllability beliefs to be stored within the same cortical territory that computes and acts on controllability signals online. A 2026 neuroimaging study compares self- and other-related mentalizing (Figure) 23. The study compares self- and other-related activity (Figure).

mPFC does not operate in isolation but as the anterior midline hub of the default mode network (DMN)–a large-scale network (mPFC, posterior cingulate cortex/precuneus, angular gyrus/TPJ, hippocampal formation, lateral temporal cortex) that is reliably active during internally directed cognition: self-reflection, autobiographical memory retrieval, prospective simulation, and mentalizing 6, 7. The DMN’s functional profile is significant because constructing and maintaining a generalized self-model of controllability requires exactly the operations this network supports: retrieving episodic evidence of past control successes and failures (hippocampal autobiographical retrieval), simulating counterfactual scenarios to evaluate what one could have done (prospective/counterfactual simulation in mPFC–hippocampal circuits), and integrating these into context-abstracted summaries (midline convergence zones) 8, 9. The DMN thus provides the network-level scaffold for the meta-cognitive self-model: hippocampal episodic stores supply the evidence base (specific episodes of experienced controllability), while mPFC and posterior midline structures abstract across episodes to maintain and revise the trait-level prior.

The hierarchy between trait-level and domain-specific priors maps onto the well-documented rostro-caudal abstraction gradient in prefrontal cortex: more posterior prefrontal regions (premotor, caudal lateral PFC) represent concrete, context-bound action-outcome contingencies, while progressively more anterior regions (rostral lateral PFC, frontopolar cortex, and medial PFC) represent increasingly abstract, temporally extended, and context-general rules and policies 10, 11, 12. In a hierarchical Bayesian framing, domain-specific empowerment priors P(ℰ∣domain)P(\mathcal{E} \mid \text{domain}) would be maintained in mid-level prefrontal and cingulate representations (encoding controllability expectations for specific task contexts or skill domains), while the most abstract trait-level prior P(ℰ)P(\mathcal{E})–corresponding to generalized self-efficacy or locus of control–would reside in the most anterior/medial prefrontal representations, consistent with frontopolar and anterior mPFC involvement in the most abstract levels of self-referential and metacognitive evaluation 13, 14.

For (c), the learning rate / precision-weighting problem–how readily the trait-level prior updates from new controllability evidence–is governed by the same hierarchical precision mechanisms that operate throughout the predictive-processing hierarchy (see “Representing Uncertainty,” “Neuromodulators”). In hierarchical Bayesian terms, the trait-level prior updates slowly when it is held with high precision (strong confidence →\rightarrow low learning rate) and rapidly when precision is low (uncertainty about self-efficacy →\rightarrow high learning rate). Neuromodulatory systems exert direct control over this: serotonergic signaling from DRN–the same system gated by vmPFC’s controllability assessment in bullet (7)–modulates the balance between perseverative and flexible behavioral strategies and is strongly implicated in setting affective priors on environmental controllability (with chronic serotonergic dysregulation linked to the “learned helplessness” phenotype and depressive attribution styles) 1, 15. Noradrenergic (LC-NE) modulation of network gain controls how much novel evidence “breaks through” existing priors–phasic NE responses to unexpected controllability changes (per bullet 7c) can transiently increase the learning rate of the meta-estimate, while tonic NE levels set the background balance between prior-dominated and evidence-dominated inference 16, 17. The pathological extremes described in the parent bullet follow naturally: depression/learned helplessness corresponds to an excessively precise (low-learning-rate) trait prior P(ℰ)≈δ(0)P(\mathcal{E}) \approx \delta(0), maintained by serotonergic/habenular dysregulation that renders the prior resistant to disconfirming evidence 1, 18, while fragile/unstable self-efficacy corresponds to an imprecise prior with excessive learning rate, vulnerable to collapse from single negative episodes. A 2025 human imaging study tests probability and confidence estimates (Figure) 24. The study maps fMRI signals associated with confidence (Figure).

The evolutionary architectural priors are: (i) the medial prefrontal cortex as a phylogenetically conserved midline structure (mammalian mPFC/vmPFC has homologues–though with debated functional equivalence–across rodents, and medial pallial territories are identifiable in non-mammalian vertebrates) that is genetically wired to integrate controllability-monitoring outputs with self-referential encoding and value computation 19, 5; (ii) the DMN-like resting-state architecture, which has been identified (with appropriate caveats about cross-species functional interpretation) in non-human primates and rodents, suggesting that the large-scale network topology linking midline self-referential hubs with hippocampal memory systems is a conserved mammalian connectivity blueprint rather than a human novelty 20, 21; (iii) the rostro-caudal prefrontal gradient, whose laminar and connectivity organization is established by genetically specified molecular gradients during development, providing the structural scaffold for hierarchical abstraction without specifying the content of any particular prior 22; and (iv) the neuromodulatory wiring (vmPFC→\rightarrowDRN, LC projections to PFC, habenula→\rightarrowmonoamine nuclei) that couples controllability-monitoring circuits to the precision-control machinery governing meta-estimate update rates. The organism thus arrives with the representational format and update architecture for a hierarchical self-model of controllability–not with any particular belief about its own efficacy, but with the structural guarantee that experienced controllability will be abstracted, cached at multiple levels of generality, and maintained with neuromodulatorily regulated confidence, enabling the rapid developmental emergence of self-efficacy beliefs from early contingency-learning episodes.
